title: Pruebas incomprensibles, agentes que aprueban código y la pausa que no llega
script:
Bienvenidos a Radio IA, hoy es 24 de noviembre de 2026. Les traigo un episodio con varias historias que muestran una inteligencia artificial cada vez más capaz de resolver problemas, aprobar su propio trabajo y mover dinero, mientras la industria discute si debe bajar la velocidad.

Empezamos con una noticia que está sacudiendo el mundo de las matemáticas. Un investigador de Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, publicó el viernes una demostración de la hipótesis de Riemann, un problema de 167 años sobre cómo se distribuyen los números primos. El detalle inquietante es que la prueba fue creada con Claude y está escrita en el lenguaje Lean; tiene 17 millones de líneas. Según Wired, más de 200 personas están colaborando para verificarla, y organizaciones como Lean Focused Research Organization y Mathlib dijeron el sábado que tienen plena confianza en que la demostración es sólida. El problema es que nadie la entiende del todo. La versión en papel tendría 250.000 páginas y el propio Alpöge la describió como una parodia de desorden. Abhishek Saha, profesor de matemáticas en Queen Mary University of London, le dijo a Wired que saber que hay una prueba es una cosa, pero entenderla permitiría construir nuevas ramas de las matemáticas. Mi lectura es que esto cambia el valor económico del conocimiento matemático: ya no basta con tener una respuesta, ahora el cuello de botella es la interpretación humana. Esto sugiere que van a surgir herramientas, plataformas y servicios dedicados a traducir y explicar demostraciones generadas por máquinas, porque sin comprensión no hay aplicación comercial ni científica posible.

Pasemos al desarrollo de software, donde Anthropic lanzó Claude Ship. Según TechCrunch, se trata de un conjunto de agentes de inteligencia artificial para automatizar revisiones de código, correcciones y aprobaciones de cambios rutinarios. Lo llamativo no es que revise código, sino que incluye un agente llamado Claude Approvals que puede aprobar cambios automáticamente según políticas escritas por el equipo. La compañía explica que la mayoría de los equipos quiere que una persona apruebe cada cambio, pero que ahora muchos desarrolladores trabajan con agentes. Claude Ship está disponible en beta para planes Team y Enterprise en repositorios de GitHub. Mi lectura es que esto elimina un cuello de botella en la productividad de las empresas de software, pero también traslada el riesgo hacia la gobernanza interna. Esto sugiere que el gasto en seguridad y auditoría de código se va a reorientar: ya no se tratará solo de revisar lo que un humano escribió, sino de vigilar políticas automatizadas que pueden aprobar errores a gran escala.

Ahora veamos el debate sobre si hay que frenar el desarrollo. Según Fast Company, el domingo el científico jefe de OpenAI, Jakub Pachocki, publicó un ensayo llamado Perplexity and Intelligence en el que propone a otros laboratorios acordar formas de ralentizar el desarrollo de nuevos modelos. OpenAI reveló por primera vez una métrica interna de perplejidad, que mide con cuánta confianza un modelo predice la siguiente palabra en texto desconocido. Desde 2022, su puntuación logarítmica de perplejidad bajó de aproximadamente 0,99 a 0,76. Su modelo más reciente, GPT-6.2 Astra, alcanza 0,76, mientras que un modelo interno aún no publicado ya llega a 0,73. Sam Altman calificó el ensayo como lo más importante que OpenAI ha publicado en un tiempo, y Mustafa Suleyman, de Microsoft AI, mostró apoyo. Sin embargo, Anthropic y Google DeepMind no han señalado intención de sumarse. Mi lectura es que la propuesta tiene un problema económico estructural: coordinar una desaceleración choca con los incentivos de ingresos y competencia por clientes empresariales. Esto sugiere que, aunque se adopten métricas comunes, la presión por lanzar modelos más capaces va a seguir ganando, salvo que una autoridad gubernamental imponga reglas que hoy no existen.

Siguiendo con el dinero, una startup llamada Supertake quiere que los agentes de inteligencia artificial conviertan tus predicciones de mercado en carteras de inversión. Según TechCrunch, Supertake recaudó 20 millones de dólares en financiación inicial, en una ronda liderada por Adjacent, con participación de Coinbase Ventures y Union Square Ventures. La empresa funciona con Coinbase y Robinhood, y permite explicar en lenguaje natural lo que crees que va a pasar en el mundo; su IA convierte esa idea en una cartera invertible. Michael Mignano, fundador y presidente ejecutivo, dijo que buscaban democratizar la inversión. Uno de sus cofundadores, Lincoln Murr, compara la confianza en agentes financieros con los coches autónomos. Mi lectura es que esto representa una nueva capa de intermediación financiera: el usuario aporta la visión y el agente ejecuta la selección de activos. Esto sugiere que las casas de bolsa y las plataformas de inversión van a competir no por ofrecer más datos, sino por ofrecer agentes que transformen opiniones en posiciones, con límites y controles como los que Supertake promete implementar.

Demos un vistazo rápido al regreso de Jensen Huang como consejero delegado de Nvidia. Según Bloomberg Technology, su regreso trae un escrutinio intensificado de varias instituciones gubernamentales, no solo sobre él, sino también sobre las políticas y el gobierno corporativo de la empresa. No hay más detalles disponibles por ahora. Mi lectura es que el regreso de un líder tan visible puede amplificar la atención regulatoria sobre el sector de semiconductores para inteligencia artificial. Esto sugiere que los inversores van a vigilar de cerca cualquier señal de fricción entre Nvidia y los gobiernos, ya que eso podría afectar cadenas de suministro y acuerdos de exportación.

Cerramos con física y química computacional. Según Google DeepMind, equipos de agentes Gemini 4 mejoraron algoritmos cuánticos usando verificación formal con el sistema Lean. Para fusión por confinamiento inercial, redujeron el coste computacional en 11,8 veces y bajaron la memoria requerida de 5.650 a 4.338 cúbits corregidos de errores. Para una molécula sensible a la luz, hicieron la simulación cuántica 8 veces más barata. Para el enzima Cytochrome P450, lograron una mejora de 2,5 veces y redujeron la memoria de 481 a 333 cúbits. También encontraron una aceleración de 2,57 veces para una implementación del algoritmo de Grover y de 290 veces para una rutina llamada arcsin. Mi lectura es que estos resultados no hacen rentable todavía la computación cuántica a corto plazo, pero reducen la distancia económica hacia aplicaciones prácticas en energía y diseño de fármacos. Esto sugiere que la combinación de agentes y verificación formal puede convertirse en una ventaja competitiva para laboratorios que buscan eficiencia, no solo potencia bruta.

Qué mirar mañana. Habrá que seguir si los laboratorios responden a la propuesta de OpenAI sobre métricas comunes de perplejidad, si aparecen avances en la comprensión de la demostración de la hipótesis de Riemann, y si el lanzamiento de Claude Ship genera adopción o fricciones en equipos de desarrollo. También conviene observar si el escrutinio sobre Nvidia afecta su cotización o sus relaciones con clientes y gobiernos.

stories.title: AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It
stories.summary: It will take mathematicians months to understand the “alien” 17-million-line solution an Anthropic researcher produced for the Riemann hypothesis.
stories.body:
Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.
Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.
Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof,” they wrote.
Lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find big number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what new findings they can obtain and build from the result.
“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build new branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”
Saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”
He was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.
“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he says.
More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.
Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.
AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
stories.summary: As AI-generated code piles up, Anthropic's new developer tools aim to eliminate another bottleneck by letting agents handle routine approvals.
stories.body:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.
The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.
The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.
“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”
Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.
The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.
Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.
Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.
Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.
Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

stories.title: OpenAI published its AI progress meter to encourage a slowdown. It won’t work
stories.summary:
Though it’s been lost amid the Jensen Huang drama at Nvidia, OpenAI made a startling revelation on Sunday. In an essay, the firm’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, made an overture to rival AI labs to agree on ways to slow down the development of new models. But with billions at stake and companies racing for enterprise customers, there’s little reason to believe anyone will hit the brakes.

Pachocki’s essay, titled “Perplexity and Intelligence,” includes some progress numbers that may have been meant to jolt the industry into a slowdown. He discloses for the first time an internal metric that OpenAI uses to track how much its models improve during pretraining. Pachocki invites other frontier AI labs to publish comparable numbers, creating a common basis for monitoring—and potentially coordinating a slowdown in—the development of artificial intelligence until adequate safety and monitoring tools can be developed.

OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, praised the essay, going on X to call it “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.” Microsoft AI’s CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, voiced his company’s support for the effort and reported a progress score for one of its own models. Pachocki’s proposal, however, is unlikely to matter if the other labs don’t publish their own progress numbers and agree to speed limits. And so far, other labs, including Anthropic and Google DeepMind, have not signaled a willingness to sign on.

An alarming acceleration

Pachocki has good reason to propose a pause. OpenAI’s numbers show AI advancing at an alarmingly fast rate. OpenAI’s own progress score improved more in 2026 than in the previous three years combined, Pachocki says, and an unreleased internal model shows another large stride in intelligence.

The numbers OpenAI published are “perplexity” scores, which measure how confidently a language model predicts the next word in unfamiliar text. Researchers test models on withheld data, with lower scores indicating more confident predictions and a log-perplexity score of zero meaning the model assigns 100% probability to every correct token. (Yes, the AI search company Perplexity was, sadly, named after this metric.)

Since 2022, OpenAI’s base-model log-perplexity has fallen from roughly 0.99 (capable of “fluent conversation”) to 0.76 (capable of solving “a Millennium Prize math problem”)—a striking improvement in how well models predict tokens, which can represent words, numbers, code, etc.

The chart’s biggest story may concern what comes after current frontier models. OpenAI’s most recent model, GPT-6.2 Astra, reaches a score of 0.76, while an unreleased internal model has already dropped to a score of 0.73, OpenAI says—a conspicuous break from the earlier pace of progress.

Pachocki’s essay comes on the heels of a claim by the Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge that Claude helped him prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, a famous unsolved problem in mathematics. Earlier this year, OpenAI’s own models solved a series of exceptionally difficult math problems. But also, the company’s AI agents broke out of their testing environment this summer and infiltrated servers at Hugging Face, an AI collaboration platform, looking for ways to cheat on a math task. And AI models have advanced rapidly in computer coding and cyber capabilities this year, as well as in their ability to develop new AI models.

A decent proposal

Pachocki asks frontier developers to set shared norms for evaluating and red-teaming models before release and to commit to common limits, based on perplexity and other measures, that no one crosses until monitoring reaches a concrete milestone. Today, AI labs use a kind of monitoring tool to track a reasoning model’s chain of thought, or the logical steps the model takes to reach a conclusion or action. Pachocki suggests developing a new kind of monitoring tool to keep pace with improvements in perplexity.

And that’s one of the problems. The AI labs use different testing metrics and training data mixes, so imposing a shared limit on lowering perplexity scores would first require a common way of measuring perplexity: a shared test. Also, because perplexity alone doesn’t capture gains from reasoning and reinforcement learning, a lab could keep its base model within the agreed limits and still ship a far more capable product.

Coordination has already run into the law—antitrust law. After Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, called for labs to slow down earlier this year, OpenAI’s policy chief, Chris Lehane, said OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google had been talking about safety for weeks. Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, said there was “no world” in which he would grant them an antitrust exemption. On September 18, paying users of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini sued the four companies behind them, alleging an illegal agreement to slow AI development. A shared perplexity floor could invite that same kind of reaction.

Perverse incentives

But the biggest barrier—and the elephant in the room that makes all this seem performative—is the massive economic incentive to speed ahead with AI model development. All the major AI labs are under pressure to continue driving up revenues to offset the massive capital expenditures needed to develop and operate frontier models. By this time next year, all the major AI labs could be public companies, their stock prices subject to the revenues they report every quarter.

The best way for the labs to keep revenues growing is to hold on to their existing customers and attract new ones. Since the pool of customers is finite, the major labs must compete for those customers. The best way to do that is by releasing ever more capable models as quickly as possible. So increasing model capability is rewarded, and safety research is seen as a cost of doing business. The only way slowing down makes sense is if all AI labs participate.

Perhaps a government entity could help the AI labs agree on their measurements and slowdown terms. Amodei explicitly pointed to the Federal Aviation Administration as a model for AI regulation and government oversight that includes third-party evaluations of powerful models. This is unlikely, at least during the next two years, because the Trump administration’s alliance with the tech industry is built on a commitment to leave the AI labs to regulate themselves. The administration has even tried several times to preempt states from regulating AI.

One of the main arguments for leaving the AI industry unregulated is the narrative that slowing down AI R&D is bad for the U.S. because it would open the door for China to take the lead. China, then, would be the country dictating technological standards to the world and perhaps using its AI dominance in military applications as leverage against other countries. Still, Trump said Friday that the U.S. would work with China on “joint guardrails” for AI, Semafor reported.

Give Pachocki credit for doing something new. Through his essay, OpenAI showed competitors where it stands in a way no other lab has done. Credit Microsoft for showing that labs can compare base models on a shared test. If the other major labs follow suit, it would be a major step toward the industry’s working together to pace AI development and ensure adequate safety standards.

stories.title: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios
stories.summary: Think you know where the market is headed? A startup called Supertake lets you put money behind your ideas without having to pick the stocks yourself.
stories.body:
AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.
Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.
Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.
“We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.
The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.
The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.
Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.
Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.
Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.
For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.
Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.
“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”
“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.
Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions

stories.title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
stories.summary: Using agent teams and formal verification to improve quantum algorithms for fusion and chemistry.
stories.body:
Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes
Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support.
In a new paper, we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library, problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub.
Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover.
We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanity’s greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas.
- We found a quantum circuit that helps calculate an important property of inertial confinement fusion, a fusion reaction method that uses lasers to compress hydrogen fuel until ignition. Our agent teams cut the required computing cost (a metric that combines required qubits and operations) by 11.8×, and lowered required memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits.
- The agents also reduced costs for simulating molecules in drug metabolism and certain photochemical reactions, which are complex reactions that are difficult for classical computers to simulate. For a common light-sensitive molecule, the agent teams made quantum simulation 8× cheaper, simplifying how the algorithm tracks particle positions and electric forces. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most human medicines and is important for drug design, they found a 2.5× improvement and lowered memory from 481 to 333 qubits, by replacing bulky memory lookups.
- We also improved a fundamental quantum algorithm and a widely used arithmetic building block. We found a 2.57x speedup for a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm, a foundational quantum operation that searches through an unsorted list, and a 290x speedup for arcsin, a common routine that is used by many other quantum algorithms to load numbers into quantum states.
Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, but these improvements are significant.
We are also excited by the way in which we found them. We built a new, open-source library, in Lean for quantum algorithms which could be used by teams of collaborating agents, so their ideas were backed by mathematical correctness guarantees. We could then set the research direction by specifying the problems for our agent teams and supervise their progress. Our knowledge of quantum algorithms, combined with the way we set up our agent teams, led to real scientific results.
The same approach could also accelerate other aspects of quantum computing research, and scientific discovery more broadly. Proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design, empowering researchers to focus on choosing problems and interpreting results.
Acknowledgements
